"Crying in the Chapel" is a song written by Artie Glenn and recorded by his son Darrell Glenn. The song was released in 1953 and reached number six on the Billboard  chart.

The song has also been recorded by many artists including the Orioles and June Valli, but the most successful version was by Elvis Presley, whose recording reached number three in the US, and number one in the UK in 1965.

sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext:
According to Artie Glenn's youngest son, Larry, the song was inspired by a personal experience his father had, and the chapel in the title was the Loving Avenue Baptist Church in [[Fort Worth, Texas]].<ref name=jones /> By this account, Glenn had suffered a serious back problem, and while in hospital, he bargained with God that he would become a better person if God helped him recover. He recuperated from a successful spinal surgery, and when he was released from hospital, he went to pray at the nearest chapel he could find. While in the chapel, he started shedding tears of joy, which was witnessed by the pastor.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2dgJVseZAlsC&pg=PA57 |title=Music of the postwar era|first= Don |last=Tyler |date= 2008 |isbn=9780313341915 |publisher=Greenwood Press |page=57 }}</ref> The inspiration for the song then came to him,<ref name=jones>{{cite news |url= https://www.newspaperarchive.com/us/texas/odessa/odessa-american/1998/04-04/page-12/ |title= 'A Song And A Prayer |first=Jim |last=Jones |date=April 4, 1998 |work=Odessa American|via=Newspaper Archive }}</ref> by the time he was back home, he had the basic tune and the chorus, and that evening he finished the rest of the song.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9hQyj7GVG1oC&pg=PA199 |page=199 |title=Untold Gold: The Stories Behind Elvis's #1 Hits|first= Ace|last= Collins |date= 2005 |isbn=9781569765074|publisher=Chicago Review Press}}</ref> 

Glenn's son Darrell recorded a demo of the song. The song, however, was rejected by a number of publishers,<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CE8xiT3pV6QC&pg=PT645 |title=Handbook of Texas Music |date=2012 |isbn=9780876112977|publisher=Texas State Historian Association}}</ref>  and the song sat unreleased for some time. The song was eventually published by Valley Publishers, while a small independent label [[Valley Records]] from Knoxville released the recording as a single.<ref name="billboard august 1953"/>
sections.text:
According to Artie Glenn's youngest son, Larry, the song was inspired by a personal experience his father had, and the chapel in the title was the Loving Avenue Baptist Church in Fort Worth, Texas. By this account, Glenn had suffered a serious back problem, and while in hospital, he bargained with God that he would become a better person if God helped him recover. He recuperated from a successful spinal surgery, and when he was released from hospital, he went to pray at the nearest chapel he could find. While in the chapel, he started shedding tears of joy, which was witnessed by the pastor. The inspiration for the song then came to him, by the time he was back home, he had the basic tune and the chorus, and that evening he finished the rest of the song. 

Glenn's son Darrell recorded a demo of the song. The song, however, was rejected by a number of publishers,  and the song sat unreleased for some time. The song was eventually published by Valley Publishers, while a small independent label Valley Records from Knoxville released the recording as a single.

sections.heading: 1953 releases
sections.wikitext:
[[Darrell Glenn]] was the first to record the song while still in high school, backed by his father's band the Rhythm Riders.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hillbilly-music.com/artists/story/index.php?id=12491 |title=Darrell Glenn |work=Hillbilly-music dawt com  }}</ref> This original version of the song was issued in May 1953.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EQ0EAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA138 |title= Coming Up in the Trade. Country & Western|magazine= Billboard|date= May 23, 1953|page= 138}}</ref>  The song became a local hit in Fort Worth, Texas,<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ow0EAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA41 |title=This Week's Territorial Best Sellers to Watch |magazine= Billboard |date= June 6, 1953 |page=41 }}</ref> and then it went nationwide.  It quickly gained the attention of other artists who then recorded the song.<ref name=leszczak />

Many different versions of the song in a variety of genres were released in the summer of 1953, and they appeared in multiple genre charts.<ref name="billboard august 1953"/><ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bQoEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA17 |title=Demarcation Lines Are Growing Hazy |page=15 |magazine=Billboard |date=September 12, 1953 |first=Bob |last=Rolontz }}</ref> Four versions (Glenn, [[Rex Allen]], [[the Orioles]] and [[June Valli]]) reached ''Billboard''{{'}}s best-selling popular records chart at the same time in August, while two versions (Glenn, Allen) also reached the country and western best-selling record chart, and one (the Orioles) on the rhythm and blues chart in the same month.<ref name="billboard august 1953">{{cite magazine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1QoEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA1 |title='Chapel' Hits Seven Positions on BB's Best-Seller Charts |magazine=Billboard |pages= 1, 18|date=August 22, 1953 }}</ref> [[Ella Fitzgerald]] and the Ray Charles Singers also recorded a Jazz version (flip side of her "When the Hands of the Clock Pray at Midnight", Decca 28762), while [[Sister Rosetta Tharpe|Rosetta Tharpe]] recorded a spiritual version. All versions sold over a combined million copies by August 1953 before they peaked in the charts.<ref name="billboard august 1953"/>

Glenn's original recording was the first to appear in ''Billboard''{{'}}s Top Popular Records as well as the country and western charts in July 1953,<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XAoEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA40 |title= Top Popular Records: Best Selling Singles|magazine=Billboard |page=40 |date=July 18, 1953 }}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XwoEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA49 |title= Top C&W Records: Most Played by Jockeys|magazine=Billboard |page=49 |date=July 25, 1953 }}</ref> eventually reaching number six on ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' pop singles chart,<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YQoEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA38 |title= Top Popular Records |magazine=Billboard |date= September 26, 1953 |page=38}}</ref> and number four on the ''Billboard'' country and western chart. The version by [[Rex Allen]] reached number eight, [[the Orioles]]' number 11, [[Ella Fitzgerald]] number 15, and Art Lund reached number 23.<ref>''Joel Whitburn's Pop Memories 1890-1954''</ref>  On the ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]'' chart where versions by Glenn, [[June Valli]],  [[the Orioles]] and [[Rex Allen]]  were amalgamated, the song reached number one.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://tropicalglen.com/Archives/50s_files/19530926.html |title=The Cash Box Best Selling Singles: Week ending September 26, 1953|work=tropicalglen.com }}</ref> In the UK, [[Lee Lawrence]] took his version to number 7.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.officialcharts.com/search/singles/crying-in-the-chapel/|title=crying in the chapel | full Official Chart History | Official Charts Company|website=www.officialcharts.com}}</ref><ref name="British Hit Singles & Albums">{{cite book
| first= David
| last= Roberts
| year= 2006
| title= [[British Hit Singles & Albums]]
| edition= 19th
| publisher= Guinness World Records Limited 
| location= London
| isbn= 1-904994-10-5
| page= 314}}</ref>

[[June Valli]] recorded her version with an orchestra directed by Joe Reisman in New York City on June 11, 1953.  [[RCA Victor Records]] released it as a single in the U.S. (catalog umber 20–5368). and elsewhere by [[EMI]] on the [[His Master's Voice (British record label)|His Master's Voice]] label (catalog number B. 10568). This was the most successful pop version on the [[Billboard charts|''Billboard'' charts]] in 1953, peaking at number four charting for a total of 17 weeks beginning August 1, 1953.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NP6OdDrutyAC&pg=PA39|title=Hit Records, 1950-1975 |first= David F. |last=Lonergan|date= 2005|page=39 |isbn=9780810851290|publisher=Scarecrow Press |language=en}}</ref> Valli's version was the 24th best-selling song of 1953,<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=awoEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA29 |title= 1953's Top Popular Records |magazine=Billboard |date=December 19, 1953 |page= 29}}</ref> while the song itself was ranked 10th in 1953's top tune.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=awoEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA28 |title= 1953's Top Tune |magazine=Billboard |date=December 19, 1953 |page= 28}}</ref> 

The doo-wop version recorded by [[the Orioles]] was the group's biggest success in the charts and their only million seller. The Orioles' version went to number one on the R&B chart and number eleven on the pop chart.<ref>{{cite book |title= Top R&B/Hip-Hop Singles: 1942-2004|last=Whitburn |first=Joel |author-link=Joel Whitburn |year=2004 |publisher=Record Research |page=444}}</ref> It became one of the best-known versions and was included on the [[41 Original Hits from the Soundtrack of American Graffiti|soundtracks]] of a number of films, including ''[[American Graffiti]]'' in 1973, ''[[Just Cause (film)|Just Cause]]'' in 1995, and ''[[Revolutionary Road (film)|Revolutionary Road]]'' in 2008.<ref name=leszczak>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hj0fAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA50 |title= Who Did It First? Great Pop Cover Songs and Their Original Artists|first= Bob |last=Leszczak |date= 2014 |page= 49–50|isbn= 9781442230682 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield Publishers }}</ref><ref name=jones />

The song was among the first songs to receive a Million-Airs award from BMI in 1979 for over a million airplays.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_iQEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PT2 |title= Songs With Million Play Get BMI's Recognition  |magazine=Billboard |date=May 26, 1979 |page= 3}}</ref>
sections.text:
Darrell Glenn was the first to record the song while still in high school, backed by his father's band the Rhythm Riders. This original version of the song was issued in May 1953.  The song became a local hit in Fort Worth, Texas, and then it went nationwide.  It quickly gained the attention of other artists who then recorded the song.

Many different versions of the song in a variety of genres were released in the summer of 1953, and they appeared in multiple genre charts. Four versions (Glenn, Rex Allen, the Orioles and June Valli) reached Billboard{{'}}s best-selling popular records chart at the same time in August, while two versions (Glenn, Allen) also reached the country and western best-selling record chart, and one (the Orioles) on the rhythm and blues chart in the same month. Ella Fitzgerald and the Ray Charles Singers also recorded a Jazz version (flip side of her "When the Hands of the Clock Pray at Midnight", Decca 28762), while Rosetta Tharpe recorded a spiritual version. All versions sold over a combined million copies by August 1953 before they peaked in the charts.

Glenn's original recording was the first to appear in Billboard{{'}}s Top Popular Records as well as the country and western charts in July 1953, eventually reaching number six on Billboard pop singles chart, and number four on the Billboard country and western chart. The version by Rex Allen reached number eight, the Orioles' number 11, Ella Fitzgerald number 15, and Art Lund reached number 23.  On the Cash Box chart where versions by Glenn, June Valli,  the Orioles and Rex Allen  were amalgamated, the song reached number one. In the UK, Lee Lawrence took his version to number 7.

June Valli recorded her version with an orchestra directed by Joe Reisman in New York City on June 11, 1953.  RCA Victor Records released it as a single in the U.S. (catalog umber 20–5368). and elsewhere by EMI on the His Master's Voice label (catalog number B. 10568). This was the most successful pop version on the Billboard charts in 1953, peaking at number four charting for a total of 17 weeks beginning August 1, 1953. Valli's version was the 24th best-selling song of 1953, while the song itself was ranked 10th in 1953's top tune. 

The doo-wop version recorded by the Orioles was the group's biggest success in the charts and their only million seller. The Orioles' version went to number one on the R&B chart and number eleven on the pop chart. It became one of the best-known versions and was included on the soundtracks of a number of films, including American Graffiti in 1973, Just Cause in 1995, and Revolutionary Road in 2008.

The song was among the first songs to receive a Million-Airs award from BMI in 1979 for over a million airplays.

On October 31, 1960, [[Elvis Presley]] cut a version of the song with plans to put it on his [[RCA Victor|RCA]] gospel album ''[[His Hand in Mine]]''. Three takes were recorded, but neither Elvis nor [[the Jordanaires]], who provided background vocals, were satisfied.<ref>[[Peter Guralnick|Guralnick, Peter]]. Careless Love: The Unmaking of Elvis Presley, 1st edition, Back Bay Books, 2000, p. 207, 672n</ref> Eventually, it was decided to shelve the recordings and move on.<ref>{{cite web|title='Crying in the Chapel' – Story Behind Lyrics|date=10 October 2019 |language=en|url=https://www.godupdates.com/elvis-presley-crying-in-the-chapel/|publisher=Alyssa Forsberg |access-date=11 April 2024}}</ref>

On April 6, 1965, "Crying In the Chapel" was issued on RCA's "Gold Standard Series." It became Elvis' first million seller since "[[Return to Sender (song)|Return to Sender]]" in 1962 and his greatest chart success over a six-year span.<ref>[[Joel Whitburn|Whitburn, Joel]]. The Billboard Book of Top 40 Hits, 7th edition,  Billboard Books, 2000, p. 502/503.</ref> The single hit number three on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] singles chart and topped the [[Adult Contemporary (chart)|Easy Listening chart]] for seven weeks.<ref>{{cite book|title= Top Adult Contemporary: 1961-2001|last=Whitburn|first=Joel|author-link=Joel Whitburn|year=2002|publisher=Record Research|page=196}}</ref> It was later included as a bonus track on Presley's 1967 gospel album, ''[[How Great Thou Art (Elvis Presley album)|How Great Thou Art]]''.

Presley's version also was a hit in the [[United Kingdom]], where it spent two non-consecutive weeks at number one.<ref>{{cite web|title=UK #1 Singles - 1960s|url=https://everyhit.co.uk/number2.html|website=Everyhit.co.uk|access-date=January 24, 2020}}</ref>

On October 31, 1960, Elvis Presley cut a version of the song with plans to put it on his RCA gospel album His Hand in Mine. Three takes were recorded, but neither Elvis nor the Jordanaires, who provided background vocals, were satisfied. Eventually, it was decided to shelve the recordings and move on.

On April 6, 1965, "Crying In the Chapel" was issued on RCA's "Gold Standard Series." It became Elvis' first million seller since "Return to Sender" in 1962 and his greatest chart success over a six-year span. The single hit number three on the Billboard Hot 100 singles chart and topped the Easy Listening chart for seven weeks. It was later included as a bonus track on Presley's 1967 gospel album, How Great Thou Art.

Presley's version also was a hit in the United Kingdom, where it spent two non-consecutive weeks at number one.

sections.heading: Bob Marley & the Wailers version
Other versions
sections.wikitext:
{{Cleanup section|reason=versions may not meet [[:WP:SONGCOVER]].|date=November 2019}}
More than 50 artists worldwide have released a version of "Crying in the Chapel".
* Arne Alm wrote the Swedish lyrics. Raya Avellan and Yngve Stoors Hawaiiorkester recorded "Klockorna i dalen" in Stockholm on October 10, 1953. The song was released on the 78 rpm record Cupol 4780.
* Ken Griffin recorded a version in 1953
* [[Johnny Burnette]] included it on his self-titled 1961 album
*[[Mahalia Jackson]] recorded a version in 1962 with Orchestra and Chorus conducted by Johnny Williams
* [[Little Richard]] recorded a version in 1963 for Atlantic Records, which became a "Regional" hit on the Billboard Chart
* [[Carol Fran]] recorded a version in 1964 for Port Records
* [[The Platters]] recorded a version in 1964 for Mercury Records
* [[Santo & Johnny]] included the song on their 1964 album, ''In the Still of the Night''
* In 1965, the Argentinian vocal group "Los 5 Latinos" with Estela Raval on the leading voice, recorded a Spanish version of the song, entitled "Llorando en la capilla", included in their album, ''El Show. Vol. 2''
* In 1965, Taiwanese singer Chen Lee Qing recorded the Chinese version of the song titled 教堂淚影. One year later Singaporean singer [[Huang Qing Yuan]] also recorded the same Chinese version of the song.
* In 1966 the Venezuelan singer Mirtha Perez made a local hit of this song in her first album as soloist, ''Mirtha Solita'', entitled "Llorando en la capilla", with arrangements by the director Jose Gay and using as background vocals the members of group "Hermanos O Brien", after, Las 4 monedas
* [[Don McLean]] recorded a version of the song on his ''[[Homeless Brother]]'' album (1974)
* [[Allies (band)|Allies]], a [[Christian rock]] band, recorded a version of the song on their album, ''Long Way From Paradise'' (1989)
